chapter: Building the band in New York
title: Heads versus arrangements in the early band
summary: Basie says the early band had only three or four arrangements and played stocks and heads, and that with larger sections written arrangements become necessary.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Buck now, "I was with Basie from '36 until I went into the Army in '43. It was different at the beginning.

When we first started out, we didn't have good arrangers writing just for the band. We used heads we made up on the job for the first four years or so and then we began to get arrangements too." Now, I guess I'm confused. I've never understood this. Not that I'm questioning what Buck is saying, but I've never understood the difference between the arrangements and the heads and how that -- when you started using heads instead of arrangements or if you ever did use arrangements?
Well, we used arrangements. We didn't have any.
You didn't have any arrangements.
(Inaudible) three or four, you know, something like that.
You had about three or four arrangements.
We played stocks (inaudible).
Stocks. Is that what you bought, you mean?
Yeah, we'd (Inaudible) buy them in a store.
Stocks?
Music store, yeah.
That's what's called stop time?
Stock.
Stock, I see.
Go ahead.
So you'd use stocks? So you didn't have arrangements.
Not many.
Very few, very few arrangements, very few. I mean, to start, at the start of the thing, you know.
You didn't.
We didn't have many. (Inaudible). And Buck started writing for the band, too.
Yeah.
(recording interruption.)
-- started, you did.
We did a lot of things. Buck made a lot of things.
Why would you want arrangements though?

Well, when you get over a certain amount of men, you got a lot of men, you got four saxophones and five saxophones and five or six or seven brass, then you -- it's hard to just sit out and (inaudible) play well, play that kind of music, use arrangements. You know, like (inaudible).
You mean it's hard to play heads with a band?
Well, you can make up a lot of things. I mean, having some fun, but then it (Inaudible) turns out to be good, I mean, and more loose. You can just have a ball with these
things, but I mean, (inaudible) music.
What's that?
It's a hard way (inaudible) that are written. It's there. It's hard, if you change bands, if you change men, then he's in trouble.
Whereas if it's written there, it's all -- have consistency.
It's there, yeah. Where are we going from here?
